title: $77 to $777: The Mathematics of Artistic Fragmentation
excerpt: A self-portrait shattered into 24,236 pieces, prices climbing from $77 to $777. The more that sells, the less remains — and the more it costs to own a piece of the artist.
content:
Imagine you could buy a piece of the artist. Not metaphorically. Not symbolically. Literally: a fragment of his face, a sliver of his iris, a swatch of his skin, captured in oil and acrylic. It starts at $77. It ends at $777. In between lies a game of supply and demand more honest than anything this industry usually offers — one that holds up a mirror to what we are willing to pay just to become a stakeholder.

The Supply

24,236 pieces. A number that sounds like planning but looks like obsession. Each one of these pieces is a fragment of a single painting — a self-portrait that exists in order to be dismantled. The pricing structure is brutally simple: $77 to $777. Whoever shows up early gets the pick of the litter and pays the entry fee. Whoever waits has to take whatever scraps remain — and shell out ten times as much for the privilege.

This isn't a clearance strategy. It's a demonstration. An experiment in the patience and vanity of the audience. Because what's being sold here isn't art, it's mechanics. The mechanism of the market itself becomes the object of desire.

The First $77

These are the bargain hunters, the collectors with fast clicks, the curious souls who think they're scoring a deal. They walk away with abstractions no one before them has laid eyes on. Blue-green smears that may once have been the artist's cheek. Red patches that perhaps depicted his mouth. For the price of a good dinner in Berlin they acquire an original. A one-of-a-kind. A piece of flesh from the creator's imagination.

They feel the rush of first pick. The power that comes from choosing, out of 24,236 possibilities, precisely this one blue-grey rectangle that catches their eye. They think they're buying art. In reality they're buying potential. The raw material of meaning, before any meaning has been assigned.

The Final $777

This is where it turns bitter. Or hilarious. Depending on how your bank balance is doing. The leftover fragments — the no-man's-land pieces, the ones deemed too abstract, too dark, too unremarkable — now become luxury goods. $777 for a smudge of paint nobody wanted in the first place. This is no longer art collecting. This is roulette. This is the moment the market drops its mask and says: You want it because it's scarce. Not because it's beautiful.

The irony is perfect: the more undesirable the piece, the higher its price. The ugly duckling becomes the swan — not through transformation, but through depletion. Whoever buys here is buying scarcity itself. The void. The fact that almost everything is already gone.

The Logic of Scarcity

That's the joke. Or the tragedy. In the normal art world, curators decide what is valuable. Here, the algorithm of availability decides. The less there is, the more it costs. A simple economic truth, held up like a mirror to the face of the industry. Because this is exactly what happens in the galleries of Zurich, New York, and Hong Kong — only without the whiff of honesty this project puts on display.

The contemporary art scene long ago forgot that value is an invention. A consensus, a shared agreement that this thing here means more than that one over there. By laying bare this mechanism — $77 for abundance, $777 for scarcity — I LAUGH YOU turns the art system itself into a work of art. The frame around the picture is folded out of banknotes, and we all stare into it as into an abyss that smiles back at us.

The Democratization of the Elite

The classical art market is a closed club. A cartel of auction houses, collector dynasties, and museum curators who decide the life or death of a work. Something cracks open here. $77 is democratic. That's the price of a concert ticket, a new pair of sneakers, a forgettable night at a mediocre bar. Suddenly the student has exactly the same access as the investment banker — at least at the beginning.

But beware: democracy ends where scarcity begins. The first buyers are the privileged ones. They get the choice, the autonomy, the feeling of power over the object. The latecomers get the leftovers. That's no longer democracy, that's a hierarchy of timing. Show up too late and you pay the price. Or $777, to be exact.

Fragments Without Context

Each of the 24,236 pieces is, on its own, abstract. That's the crucial part. Buy a piece and you receive no information about which part of the face it once was. You get color, form, texture. The rest you project onto it. That's the real deal here: the artist isn't selling you his identity, he's selling you the space for your own interpretation.

It's radically democratic and deeply cynical at once. Democratic, because anyone — really anyone with $77 in their pocket — can become a stakeholder. Cynical, because it shows how willingly we project meaning into objects, so long as they come labeled as art. A smudge is just a smudge until someone says: this is a piece of something bigger. Then it's worth $777.

That's the subtle difference from the traditional art market. With Picasso, we know: the eye belongs to the woman, the woman to Cubism, Cubism to history. Here we know nothing. The abstraction isn't style, it's the consequence of fragmentation. A blue smear could be sky or vein. A red stroke could be lipstick or blood. Meaning emerges only in the viewer's head — and in their wallet.

The Body as Currency

Don't forget what is physically happening here. A human being painted himself. Then he dismantled himself into 24,236 pieces. Now you are buying him. Piece by piece. This is no longer metaphor. This is cannibalism within capitalism. We devour the creator while we applaud him.

This act of dismemberment is violent and tender at once. Violent, because it turns the individual into tradable units. Tender, because it allows each of those units to begin a new life. In 24,236 living rooms, offices, and collectors' basements, a piece of him will soon hang. The artist becomes omnipresent through his own destruction. A Christian motif, profaned by capitalism. Communion becomes e-commerce.

And the punchline? The more we devour, the more we want what remains. The final pieces will be the most expensive — not because they're the best, but because they're the last. That's the poetry of the market. The ugliness of scarcity. The laughter at the logic.

I LAUGH YOU — or the Irony of the Price Tag

In the end there you stand — with a fragment in your hand that cost you $77 or $777. You have bought a piece of someone you don't know. A sliver of an identity that now hangs in your living room. And you ask yourself: Is this investment? Is this love? Or is this the joke the artist is playing on all of us, while he pockets our money?

My bet is on the latter. Not out of malice, but out of despair. Because if art is nothing more than a commodity traded by the laws of supply and demand, then all we can do is laugh. Or cry. Or both — at $77 to $777 a piece.

The project shows us our own face. The face of a society ready to buy anything as long as it's sold as exclusive. Ready to pay the price simply because others can no longer afford it. $77 is an on-ramp, $777 is a velvet rope. Between them lie 24,236 decisions about who is worth what. And somewhere in between, between the first bargain and the final luxury good, the answer to the question of why we are doing any of this gets lost.
